new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Only one work is listed for koru1245 and it was opened, so the spot-check was run on the earlier-check files already in that the compiler report cites as finding nothing. One item was missed: Godschalk 1993, Sela Valley, Wordlist pp. 147-155 (PDF pages 160-168; the earlier classification's 'pp. 147-152' is short by three pages) marks lexical tone on three minimal pairs, confirmed against the page scan: p. 153 (PDF 166) 'phay 1. [high tone] multi-pronged arrow (West Sela).. 2. [falling tone] brother-in-law' and 'si 1. [high tone] name.. 2. [falling tone] tooth'; p. 155 (PDF 168) 'yim 1. [high tone] hill 2. [falling tone] male (non-human)'. The wordlist also carries grave accents on i and u i…

sources.note: Only comparative and Eipo-specific remarks: p. 12 'Stress seems to be partially phonemic in the east, e.g. Ok Bab tuku "fire" and aku "young plant of sweet potatoes", while tones are said to be phonemic in Nalca and Kosarek (Bromley 1973:15 and Rule and Cutting)'; pp. 22-23 give the Eipo stress rule (disyllables: stress on the syllable with more satellites; not word-final in open syllables after clusters; otherwise intonation-dependent; stress co-occurs with high rising tone). sources.citation: Ethnologue 22nd ed. (2019) and 14th ed. (2002), entry Korupun-Sela [kpq] (the Internet Archive copies).
sources.note: Nothing. Alternate names Kimyal of Korupun, Korapun; population 8,000 (1996 E. Young); dialects Korupun (Duram), Dagi, Sisibna (Gobugdua), Deibula, Sela; 60% lexical similarity with Nipsan; NT 2010; Latin script. No bibliography.

sources.citation: Rosetta Project. 2010. Korupun-Sela Swadesh List (kpq). archive.org.
sources.note: Nothing; ~40-item wordlist with aspirated stops (pʰ, kʰ, tʰ), no stress marks, no source named in the metadata (looks Bromley-derived).

sources.citation: Godschalk, Jan Anthonie. 1993. Sela Valley: An Ethnography of a Mek Society in the Eastern Highlands, Irian Jaya, Indonesia. PhD thesis, Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam. Geldermalsen: Logoconsult. xvi+204 pp.
sources.note: Nothing. Ethnography with a 6-page wordlist (pp. 147-152) written in a practical orthography with no stress marks and no orthography/phonology note; ch. 1 (pp. 3-5) discusses dialects (West/East Sela communalects, Hao/Weip dialect, 'Korupun Kimyal' in the Erok and Dagi valleys) and says 'Linguistic studies, including the compilation of a dictionary, have been carried out by Young (1981)'; bibliography p. 164 lists 'Young, E. 1981. Korupun Kimyal Phonemics. Unpublished manuscript, 30 pp.'; preface p. xiv thanks 'Ms. Elinor Young, whose dictionary and other linguistic write-ups became valuable…

sources.citation: Glottolog 5.3, languoid page koru1245 Korupun-Sela and kora1298 Korapun-Bromley; reference records 37015 (Heeschen 1978), 34449 (Heeschen 1992), 718700 (Suter 2021).
sources.note: Bibliographic only. koru1245 has no descriptive reference; comments on subclassification cite Heeschen 1978, Heeschen 1992 (BKI 148(3/4): 465-488, tagged Ketengban/Eipo/Kosarek Yale) and Suter 2021 (NUSA 71: 1-20). kora1298 Korapun-Bromley is treated as a separate (Bromley-wordlist) variety citing Voorhoeve 1975 and Godschalk 1993: 4.

sources.citation: Hammarström et al., hh.bib (Glottolog source bibliography, local copy _glottolog_bib/hh.bib): entries ew:Godschalk:Sela-Valley, t:Young:Kimyal (Young & Mirin 1991, Luke in Kimyal, RBMU), and the language code note on Voorhoeve 1975 ('Korapun (Br) so different from Godschalk-Sela and Kimyal-Sela of Kroneman that it must be a different language').
sources.note: Nothing on stress; confirms that the only Kimyal-language items known to Glottolog are the ethnography, a Gospel of Luke (1991) and unpublished Kroneman Kimyal-Sela wordlist data.

sources.note: States that in (West) Sela tone is phonemic in at least some monosyllabic roots, high vs falling, but that the distinction is documented for only three pairs: pháⁱ 'arrow sp.' vs phâⁱ 'brother-in-law', sí 'name' vs sî 'tooth', jɪ́m 'hill' vs jɪ̂m 'male' (Usher's retranscription of Godschalk 1993: 153, 155, where the entries read 'phay 1. [high tone].. 2. [falling tone]', 'si 1. [high tone] name 2. [falling tone] tooth', 'yim 1. [high tone] hill 2. [falling tone] male (non-human)').
